title: What plants need, and how they grow towards the light

summary.text: Turn a pot of young sprouts around, and by the next day they have bent back towards the window. A plant cannot walk to the light, so they grow towards it. Plants need light, water, air, warmth and soil to live and grow. Your child grows rai (mustard) sprouts by a window, turns one cup round, and watches what the sprouts do.
summary.art: Two paper cups of small mustard sprouts on a windowsill, one leaning towards the window and one being turned round by a child's hand.

intro.hook: Look at a plant that lives indoors, near a window. Which way are the leaves and stems leaning?
intro.text: Most plants indoors lean towards the nearest window. Nobody pulled them that way. The plant grew that way. What happens if we turn the pot round, so the plant leans away from the window? In this unit we find out. We also look at the five things a plant needs: light, water, air, warmth and soil.
intro.art: A money plant on a shelf in a flat, with all the leaves turned towards a bright window.

outcomes: By the end I can name five things a plant needs: light, water, air, warmth and soil.
By the end I can say what young sprouts do when the light comes from one side: they bend towards it.
By the end I can say what happened when we turned the cup round, and why.
By the end I can say that seeds can sprout without soil, but plants need soil, or minerals, to keep growing.
By the end I can say why roots need air as well as water.
By the end I can make a guess, give a reason, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: Phototropism is a plant growing towards light. 'Photo' means light, and 'tropism' means turning.
terms.example: Rai sprouts on a windowsill bend towards the window. That is phototropism.
terms.art: A row of small sprouts in a cup, all bending towards a bright window.

terms.meaning: The shoot is the part of a young plant that grows up out of the seed: the stem and the first leaves.
terms.example: A rai sprout's shoot is a thin white or green stem with two small leaves on top.
terms.art: A mustard sprout with a white root going down and a thin stem with two round leaves going up.

terms.meaning: To germinate is to start growing from a seed. First a tiny root comes out, then a shoot.
terms.example: Rai seeds on wet tissue germinate in one or two days in warm weather.
terms.art: Mustard seeds on wet tissue, some with tiny white roots poking out.

terms.meaning: Soil is the top layer of the ground. It is made of tiny bits of rock, bits of dead plants and animals, water and air.
terms.example: The soil in a flower pot holds the plant up and holds water for the roots.
terms.art: A glass jar of soil showing sand, small stones, dark crumbs and bits of leaf.

terms.meaning: Minerals are tiny bits from rocks that dissolve in water. Plants take them in through their roots to stay healthy.
terms.example: Farmers add manure to a field, because it puts minerals back into the soil.
terms.art: A root in damp soil, with tiny dots in the water around the root.

explanations.definition: A young shoot bends towards the brightest light. This is called phototropism.
explanations.description: A plant makes their food in their green leaves, using light, so getting the leaves into light matters a great deal. A shoot senses where the light is coming from. Then the side of the stem away from the light grows a little faster than the side facing it, so the stem bends towards the light. Turn the plant round, and the bend starts again the other way. In the grass shoots the Darwins tested, the tip sensed the light best.
examples: Rai sprouts by a window bend towards the glass within a day.
A money plant in a dim room grows long stems towards the window.
Young sunflower plants turn their heads east to west through the day, following the Sun.
explanations.context: This card explains what we saw when we turned the cup of sprouts.
explanations.art: A sprout stem drawn large, with the shady side shown with longer cells and the stem bending towards a sun.

explanations.definition: Every plant needs water to live and grow. Roots take in water from the soil.
explanations.description: Water keeps stems and leaves firm, and carries minerals up from the roots. The leaves use water, with light and air, to make food. A plant short of water wilts: the leaves go soft and droop. Different plants need different amounts. A cactus needs very little, and rice grows in fields full of water.
examples: A tulsi plant droops on a hot afternoon and stands up again after a drink.
Rice fields in Thanjavur and in Assam are kept flooded while the rice grows.
A cactus in Rajasthan can go weeks without rain.
explanations.context: This card is about water, one of the five needs of a plant.
explanations.art: A droopy plant in dry soil next to the same plant standing tall after watering.

explanations.definition: Plants need air for two jobs. Leaves take in a gas from the air called carbon dioxide to make food. Every part of a plant, roots too, takes in oxygen from the air to breathe.
explanations.description: Leaves take in carbon dioxide through tiny holes, too small to see. With light and water, they turn it into food. Roots breathe too, using oxygen from the air in the gaps between bits of soil. If soil stays soaking wet for days, water fills those gaps, and the roots can rot. That is why most pots have a hole at the bottom.
examples: Bubbles rise when you pour water on dry soil. That is the air from the gaps in the soil.
Flower pots have a hole in the bottom so extra water can drain away.
Mangrove trees in the Sundarbans grow roots that stick up out of the mud, to take in air.
explanations.context: This card is about air, one of the five needs of a plant.
explanations.art: A cut-away pot showing roots in soil, with small air gaps between the soil crumbs, and a drainage hole at the bottom.

explanations.definition: Plants grow only when it is warm enough for them. Each kind of plant has the warmth they grow best in.
explanations.description: In cold weather, seeds germinate slowly and plants grow slowly. Frost, a thin layer of ice on very cold nights, can kill the leaves of many plants. Too much heat can dry a plant out. Different plants like different warmth: rice and bananas like hot, wet weather, mustard and wheat are sown in the cool winter in the north, and apples grow in cold hills like Himachal Pradesh and Kashmir.
examples: Rai seeds sprout in a day or two in a warm Chennai kitchen. In a cold Delhi winter they can take several days longer.
Mustard fields in Punjab and Rajasthan turn yellow with flowers in winter.
Coconut palms grow along the warm coasts of Kerala and Goa, but not high in the Himalayas.
explanations.context: This card is about warmth, one of the five needs of a plant.
explanations.art: A map-like picture of India with a coconut palm on the warm coast, a yellow mustard field in the north in winter, and an apple tree in the hills.

explanations.concept: Plants need soil, or what is in it
explanations.definition: Soil holds a plant up, holds water and air for the roots, and gives the plant minerals.
explanations.description: A seed carries a small store of food inside, so seeds can germinate on wet tissue with no soil at all. But the store runs out after some days. To keep growing, a plant needs minerals, which come from the soil. Plants do not eat soil; they make their food in their leaves. Farmers can grow plants with their roots in water if they add minerals to the water. This is called hydroponics.
examples: Rai seeds sprout on wet tissue as well as in soil.
A money plant can live for months in a bottle of water, with no soil.
Some farms in Indian cities grow lettuce in pipes of water with minerals, without soil.
explanations.context: This card is about soil, one of the five needs of a plant.
explanations.art: Two cups side by side: rai sprouts on wet tissue, and rai sprouts in soil, both green.

explanations.concept: Does a sprout decide to turn?
explanations.description: Scientists agree on what happens. Light falls on one side of the shoot. A messenger chemical called auxin moves to the shady side. There it makes the stem grow faster, so the stem bends. People describe this in different ways.
examples: A rai sprout turned away from the window bends back within a day.
A potato sprouting in a dark cupboard grows a long pale shoot towards a crack of light.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how plants sense and act
perspectives.explanation: A sprout feels where the light is and grows towards it. Sensing, then acting on what you sensed, is what a mind does. A sprout does this with chemicals and cells, not a brain.
The bend is a response, set off by light and carried out by auxin. The sprout does the same thing every time, so they do not call it a decision.

explanations.context: This card is about a question people argue about: what is a sprout doing when they turn?
explanations.art: A sprout bending towards a window, with two speech bubbles from two scientists.

agreed.text: Young shoots of most plants grow towards light.
agreed.evidence: Seedlings on a windowsill bend towards the window. Charles and Francis Darwin showed in 1880 that the shoot tip senses the light. Since then, many experiments have shown the same thing.

agreed.text: Plants need light, water, air, a suitable warmth and minerals to grow.
agreed.evidence: A plant missing any one of these grows weak or dies. Farmers and gardeners everywhere see this, and scientists have tested each one.

agreed.text: Plants make their food in their leaves. They do not eat soil.
agreed.evidence: A plant grows heavy, yet the soil in the pot hardly gets lighter. Plants grow in water with minerals, with no soil at all.

challenging.claim: Plants eat soil, so the soil is their food.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Plants grow in soil, and they grow badly in poor soil.
challenging.against: Plants make their food in their leaves, from air and water, using light. From the soil they take water and small amounts of minerals. Plants can grow in water with minerals added and no soil at all.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: that plants eat soil.

challenging.claim: A sunflower in full bloom turns to follow the Sun all day.
challenging.who: A common belief, in many countries
challenging.for: Young sunflower plants really do turn their heads from east to west during the day, and back again at night.
challenging.against: Once the flowers open, most sunflowers stop turning and face east. In 2016, Stacey Harmer and her team in the United States showed that young sunflowers time their turning with an inside clock. East-facing flowers warm up faster in the morning, and bees visit them more.
challenging.context: This card is about a belief that is only half true: that sunflowers always follow the Sun.

challenging.claim: A plant bends towards the window because the light pulls the stem.
challenging.for: The stem does end up pointing at the light, as if pulled.
challenging.against: Light does not pull anything. The stem bends because the shady side grows faster than the sunny side. A pulled stem would bend at once. A growing stem takes hours, and the bend stays.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that light pulls a plant.

big_questions.q: We turned the cup, and the sprouts bent back to the window. How did they know where the window was?
big_questions.hint: Think about which part of the sprout faced the light. What can you sense without eyes?

big_questions.q: A plant moves by growing. Can you move by growing?
big_questions.hint: Think about your hair, your nails, and how tall you were last year.

big_questions.q: If a plant could walk, would they still need to bend towards light?
big_questions.hint: Animals walk to their food. Plants grow towards theirs. Which way is better? Is one better?

big_questions.q: Every plant on a windowsill leans the same way. What would plants look like on a planet with two Suns?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the sprouts did when the light came from one side, and then from the other.

big_questions.q: Light, water, air, warmth and soil all come from outside the plant. So what part of a plant is only the plant?
big_questions.hint: Think about the seed. What did the seed bring with them?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out how a plant bends towards light? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: People had long seen plants bend towards light. Many thought the part of the stem that bends is the part that senses the light. In 1880, Charles Darwin and his son Francis, in England, tested this. They grew canary grass seedlings, which have a thin shoot with a pointed tip. They put tiny black caps over the tips of some shoots, so no light could reach the tips. Those seedlings hardly bent at all. When the caps let light through, the seedlings bent towards the light as usual. When the tip was in the light but the lower stem was covered, the shoots still bent. So the tip senses the light, and something travels down from the tip to the part that bends. Nobody knew what that something was. In the 1920s, a young Dutch scientist, Frits Went, cut off shoot tips and stood them on small blocks of agar. Agar is the seaweed jelly sold in India as China grass. A block that had held tips made a cut shoot bend, all by itself. The messenger was a chemical. Today it is called auxin.
how_we_found_out.who: Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin, in England (1880); Frits Went, a Dutch scientist (1920s)
how_we_found_out.when: The Darwins published their tests in 1880, in their book The Power of Movement in Plants. Went's agar test was in the 1920s.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the part of the stem that bends is the part that senses the light. The Darwins showed that the tip senses it, and a message travels down to the part that bends.
how_we_found_out.art: A row of small grass seedlings in a pot by a window: some with tiny black caps on their tips standing straight, and the rest bending towards the light.

story.title: Meenakshi Turns the Pot
story.note: Meenakshi, Anu and Appa are made up. Mustard sprouts really do bend towards a window, and really bend back within about a day when the pot is turned.
text: Meenakshi lived in a flat in Chennai, on the fifth floor. She was seven. Her little sister Anu was five. Their kitchen had one small window, above the sink.

One morning, Meenakshi took a pinch of kadugu, the small black mustard seeds, from the masala box. She sowed them in an old steel tumbler full of soil. She pressed the seeds into the soil with her finger. She sprinkled water on top. Then she put the tumbler on the kitchen counter, beside the window.
Every morning she gave the soil one spoon of water. On the second day, tiny shoots came up. By the fourth day, each one had two small round leaves at the top.
On the fifth day, Appa was making coffee. He looked at the tumbler. 'These mustard plants are all falling over,' he said. 'The fan must have blown them.'
Meenakshi looked. All the little shoots were leaning the same way. They were not falling. They were leaning towards the window.
'The fan blows round and round, Appa,' she said. 'But they are all leaning one way. They are leaning to the window.'
'Plants cannot move,' said Appa. 'They stay where they are planted.'

Meenakshi thought about this. Then she had an idea. She put a small red bindi on the side of the tumbler that faced the window. Then she turned the tumbler round. Now the bindi faced the room, and all the shoots leaned towards the stove.
'What are you doing?' asked Anu.
'I am asking the mustard sprouts a question,' said Meenakshi. 'If they were blown by the fan, they will stay like this. If they lean to the light, they will turn back.'
'Which one will it be?' asked Anu.
'I don't know yet,' said Meenakshi. 'That's why I'm asking.'
That night, Anu peeped at the tumbler before bed. The shoots still leaned towards the stove. 'Nothing happened,' she said.
'Plants are slow,' said Meenakshi. 'Wait till morning.'

In the morning, Meenakshi ran to the kitchen. The shoots had changed. Each one had a little bend near the top. The bottom of each stem still leaned towards the stove. But the top had curved round, and the leaves pointed at the window again.
'Appa!' she called. 'Come and see!'
Appa came with his coffee. He looked at the bindi, which still faced the room. He looked at the bent shoots. 'Nobody touched them?' he asked.
'Nobody,' said Meenakshi. 'They did it themselves, in one night. A plant cannot walk to the window. So they grow towards it.'
'But how?' said Appa. 'They have no legs, and no eyes.'
'I think the side away from the window grew a bit more,' said Meenakshi. 'If one side of you grows longer, you bend. Look, the bend is right at the top, where the shoot is growing.'
Appa put his cup down. 'So the plant was moving the whole time,' he said. 'Just too slowly for me to see.'
'Can I turn it now?' asked Anu.
'Yes,' said Meenakshi. 'Turn it all the way round. And tomorrow, we'll see if the mustard turns too.'
Anu turned the tumbler very carefully. Then she leaned her own head towards the window, slowly, slowly, like a mustard shoot. Meenakshi laughed, and leaned with her.
story.epiphany: Meenakshi works out that the shoots were not blown over. When the light came from the other side, they bent back to it, by growing. A plant moves by growing.
ask: Appa thought the fan blew the plants over. How did Meenakshi's test show this was not right?
Why did Meenakshi put a bindi on the tumbler?
Why did nothing seem to happen by bedtime?
What do you think the mustard shoots felt when the light came from behind them?

A father holding a coffee tumbler, looking at small mustard shoots all leaning towards the window.
The steel tumbler with a red bindi facing the room, and the shoot tips curved round towards the window, while a small girl leans her head the same way.

experiments.title: The Turning Cup: will the sprouts turn back?
experiments.context: In this experiment you grow rai (mustard) sprouts in two cups by a window. Then you turn one cup round, so the sprouts lean away from the light. You watch what they do by the next day.
experiments.question: Rai sprouts by a window lean towards the light. If we turn the cup round, what will the sprouts do?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After we turn the cup round, will the sprouts stay leaning into the room, fall over, or turn back to the window? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both cups get the same seeds from one packet, the same soil or tissue, the same water and the same window. The only difference is that we turn cup A round and leave cup B as it is. So if cup A changes and cup B does not, the turning made the change.
results_table: Day 4: which way do the sprouts lean?
Day 5: which way do the sprouts lean?

materials.item: rai (mustard; kadugu in Tamil) seeds from the kitchen. If they do not sprout, use moong or methi.
2 small cups, such as paper cups or curd cups, the same size
soil from a pot plant, or kitchen tissue folded into 4 layers and wetted
materials.qty: enough for 2 cm in each cup

materials.item: a spoon and a cup of water
a bindi, a sticker or a pen mark, to mark one side of each cup
a window where light comes in from one side

schedule.what: Fill both cups. Scatter the rai seeds and wet them. Put both cups by the window.
Give each cup 1 spoon of water. Look for tiny white roots.
Give each cup 1 spoon of water. Look for tiny shoots.
See which way the sprouts lean. Mark the window side of each cup. Guess, then turn cup A round.
Look at both cups. Draw them. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: On day 4, draw both cups with an arrow for the way the sprouts lean. On day 5, draw them again. Draw the window in both drawings.

flow.do: 1. Write A on one cup and B on the other. 2. Fill each cup with 2 cm of soil, or wet folded tissue. 3. Scatter 1 teaspoon of rai seeds on each. 4. Sprinkle 2 spoons of water on each. 5. Put both cups side by side, by the window.
flow.say: We are going to grow rai sprouts in these two cups. Rai is the mustard we put in sambar and poriyal. Help me scatter the seeds.
flow.kid: Fill the two cups. Scatter the rai seeds on top. Sprinkle water. Put both cups by the window.
flow.parent: Use a window where light comes from one side, not from all around. A bright window with no hot sun on the cups is best. Seeds just lying on the soil are fine.

flow.do: Give each cup 1 spoon of water. Look closely at the seeds together. On day 3, do the same again and look for tiny shoots.
flow.say: Look closely. What has changed since yesterday?
flow.kid: Give each cup one spoon of water. Look closely at the seeds. What has changed?

ask.q: What do you see?
good: Tiny white roots.
The seeds have split open.

flow.parent: In warm weather rai germinates in a day or two. In a cold room it may take 3 or 4 days. Keep watering 1 spoon a day, and wait until the shoots are about 2 cm tall.

flow.do: 1. Look at the sprouts from the side. 2. Ask which way they lean. 3. Put a bindi on the side of each cup that faces the window.
flow.say: Look at the sprouts from the side. Are they standing straight? Which way are they leaning? Let's mark the window side of each cup with a bindi.
flow.kid: Look at your sprouts from the side. Which way do they lean? Put a bindi on the window side.
flow.wait: Come back when the shoots are about 2 cm tall, usually on day 4.

ask.q: Which way are the sprouts leaning?
good: Towards the window.
Towards the light.

flow.parent: The sprouts in both cups should lean towards the window. If they stand straight, the light may be coming from above. Move the cups to the side of the window, or stand them inside a shoebox lying on its side with the open end facing the window.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess what will happen if cup A is turned round. Wait for a guess and a reason. Write it down. Then let your child turn cup A round, so its bindi faces the room. Leave cup B as it is.
flow.say: Right now the sprouts in both cups lean towards the window. If we turn cup A round, they will lean away from the window. What will they do by tomorrow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. If you turn cup A round, what will the sprouts do? Why? Now turn cup A round.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: They will turn back, because they need the light.
They will stay, because plants can't move.
They will fall over.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Many children, and grown-ups, guess that the sprouts will stay leaning into the room. Do not say what will happen. Cup B is the comparison: it shows what the sprouts do when nothing is changed.

check.q: Why do we leave cup B as it is?
options: So we can compare cup A with cup B
check.why: Cup B shows what sprouts do when we change nothing. If cup A changes and cup B does not, the turning made the change.

flow.do: 1. Look at both cups from the side. 2. Look at the bindi on cup A. Is it still facing the room? 3. Look at the tops of the sprouts in cup A. 4. Draw both cups, with the window.
flow.say: Look at cup A. The bindi still faces the room. Which way are the tops of the sprouts pointing now? Now look at cup B. What is the same, and what is different?
flow.kid: Look at cup A. Which way do the tops point now? Look at cup B. Draw both cups.
flow.wait: Come back tomorrow, on day 5. If you can, also peep in the evening of day 4.

ask.q: Which way are cup A's sprouts pointing now?
good: Back to the window.
The tops have bent towards the light.

ask.q: Where is the bend on each sprout?
good: Near the top.
Just below the leaves.

check.q: We turned cup A round. The next day, which way did the tops of the sprouts point?
check.why: The sprouts sensed the light coming from behind them. They grew more on their shady side, so their tops bent back to the window.

flow.parent: Rai sprouts usually bend back within half a day to a day. The bottom of each stem still leans the old way, and the top curves round, so the stem looks like a hook. If nothing has changed, wait one more day, and check the cup is in bright light.

flow.do: Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and the reason. Then read the explanation card on light together.
flow.say: Say what you think happened. Then tell me what you saw that shows it. Then tell me why you think the sprouts did it.
flow.kid: Say what you think happened. Say what you saw. Say why the sprouts did it.

ask.q: What happened, and how do you know?
good: The sprouts turned back to the light. Cup A's tops bent to the window, but nobody touched them.
Cup B did not change, so turning the cup made cup A bend.

ask.q: How can a plant bend without legs?
good: By growing more on one side.
The side away from the window grew longer.

flow.think: A plant cannot walk to the light. What else could a plant do to reach the light?
flow.parent: A strong answer: the sprouts bent back towards the window, because they grow towards light. The proof is that cup A changed and cup B did not. The explanation card then gives the reason: the shady side of the stem grows faster.

experiments.title: Soil or No Soil? Two cups of rai
experiments.context: In this experiment you sow rai seeds in two cups. One cup has soil. The other has only wet tissue. You watch whether the seeds need soil to sprout, and what happens after a week.
experiments.question: Do rai seeds need soil to sprout? Do the sprouts need soil to keep growing?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the seeds on wet tissue sprout? After ten days, which cup will have the bigger plants? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both cups get the same seeds, the same water, and the same place by the window. The only difference is soil or tissue. We sow 10 seeds in each cup, so we can count fairly.
results_table: Day 3: how many of the 10 seeds sprouted?
Day 10: how tall? How many leaves?

materials.item: 20 rai (mustard) seeds
2 small cups the same size
soil from a pot plant, enough for 3 cm in one cup
kitchen tissue or cotton wool, enough for 4 layers in the other cup
a spoon and water

schedule.what: Fill one cup with soil and one with wet tissue. Put 10 seeds on each. Water both.
Count the sprouts in each cup.
Check both cups are damp, and add a spoon of water if they are dry. Look at the leaves.
Compare the two cups. Count the leaves on one plant in each.

experiments.record: Draw both cups on day 3 and on day 10. Write how many seeds sprouted in each.

setup.art: Two cups side by side: one filled with dark soil, one filled with white folded tissue, each with 10 small black seeds on top.
setup.caption: 1. One cup of soil, one cup of wet tissue. 10 seeds in each.

setup.art: The same two cups on day 10: both with green sprouts, the soil cup with a few slightly larger leaves.
setup.caption: 2. On day 10, compare the two cups.

flow.do: 1. Fill cup 1 with soil. 2. Fold tissue into cup 2 and wet it. 3. Count out 10 rai seeds onto each cup. 4. Sprinkle 2 spoons of water on each.
flow.say: This cup has soil. This one has only wet tissue. Will the seeds sprout without soil? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill one cup with soil. Fill one with wet tissue. Put 10 seeds on each. Guess: will both sprout? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Seeds need soil to grow.
Seeds only need water to sprout.

flow.parent: Keep the tissue damp, not swimming in water. Many children guess that the tissue seeds will not sprout.

flow.do: Count the sprouts in each cup. Write the numbers down.
flow.say: How many seeds sprouted in the soil cup? How many on the tissue? Were you right?
flow.kid: Count the sprouts in each cup. Which cup has more?
flow.wait: Come back on day 3. Each day, check that the soil and the tissue are damp, and add a spoon of water if they feel dry.

ask.q: Did the tissue seeds sprout?
good: Yes, almost as many as in the soil.

check.q: Rai seeds on wet tissue, with no soil, did what?
check.why: A seed carries a little store of food inside. With water, the seed germinates even without soil.

flow.parent: Both cups usually sprout about the same number. A seed needs water, air and warmth to germinate, but not soil.

flow.do: Water both cups with 1 spoon each. Look at the leaves.
flow.say: Look at the leaves in each cup. Do they look the same?
flow.kid: Give each cup one spoon of water. Look at the leaves.
flow.wait: Come back on day 6. Keep both cups damp in between.

flow.do: 1. Put the two cups side by side. 2. Pick one plant from each cup and count their leaves. 3. Draw both cups.
flow.say: Which cup has the bigger plants now? Why might that be?
flow.kid: Which cup has bigger plants now? Count the leaves. Why are they different?

ask.q: Why are the soil plants bigger?
good: The soil gave them something more.
The seed's food ran out on the tissue.
Soil has minerals.

flow.parent: The seed brought a little food store with them, so tell your child this only after they have given their own idea. By day 10 the soil plants usually have new, jagged leaves growing between the first two round ones. The tissue plants often stay small, and their leaves may turn pale. If the two cups still look the same, keep going a few more days. The claim: seeds sprout without soil, but plants need the minerals in soil to keep growing.

activities.title: Which Way Do Our Plants Lean?
activities.context: In this activity you look at plants in your home, on your balcony or outside your window. You find out which way each one leans, and where their light comes from.

materials.item: any plants you can see: a pot plant, a money plant, a tulsi, or a tree from the window. If you have none, look at a plant outside your window or at a shop.
materials.qty: as many as you can find

materials.item: paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Find plants. See which way they lean. Draw an arrow from each plant to their light.

activities.record: Draw a simple map of one room. Draw each plant and the window. Draw an arrow for the way each plant leans.

setup.art: A child crouching beside a money plant on a shelf, pointing at the leaves turned towards a window.
setup.caption: 1. Find a plant. Look at the leaves and stems.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a room with a window and three plants, each with an arrow pointing to the window.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the room, the window, and an arrow for each plant.

flow.do: 1. Walk round your home with your child. 2. Stop at each plant. 3. Look at which way the leaves face and the stems lean.
flow.say: Let's look at our plants like detectives. Which way are this plant's leaves facing? Where is the window?
flow.kid: Find a plant at home. Which way do the leaves face? Where is the window?

ask.q: Do the plants all lean the same way?
good: Most lean to the window.
The ones near the window lean to it.

flow.parent: Indoor plants nearly always lean or face towards the brightest window. A plant in the middle of a sunny balcony may stand straight, because light comes from many sides.

flow.do: Draw the room together. Draw each plant, the window, and an arrow for the way each one leans.
flow.say: Let's draw the room. Where is the window? Draw an arrow for each plant. What do you notice about the arrows?
flow.kid: Draw the room and the window. Draw an arrow for each plant. Where do the arrows point?
flow.think: Did someone push the plants to face the window? Or did they grow that way?

activities.title: Soil in a Glass: find the air and the bits
activities.context: In this activity you pour water on dry soil and watch for bubbles. Then you stir the soil in water and let it settle overnight. You find out what soil is made of.

materials.item: 2 clear glasses or jam jars
dry soil from a pot, or from the ground below your building
water
a spoon

schedule.what: Pour water on dry soil and watch for bubbles. Stir soil in water in the second glass and leave it.
Look at the layers in the second glass.

activities.record: Draw the bubbles in glass 1. On day 2, draw the layers in glass 2 and label them.

setup.art: A child slowly pouring water onto dry soil in a clear glass, with bubbles rising through the soil.
setup.caption: 1. Pour water slowly onto dry soil. Watch for bubbles.

setup.art: A glass jar of muddy water the next day, settled into layers: small stones at the bottom, sand, fine mud, clear water, and bits of leaf floating on top.
setup.caption: 2. Stir soil in water. Next day, look for layers.

flow.do: 1. Fill glass 1 one-third full with dry soil. 2. Let your child pour water in slowly, down the side. 3. Watch the soil closely.
flow.say: Pour the water slowly. Watch the soil. What comes up?
flow.kid: Pour the water slowly onto the soil. Watch closely. What comes up?

ask.q: Where did the bubbles come from?
good: There was air in the soil.
Air in the gaps between the bits.

flow.parent: Bubbles rise because water fills the gaps between the soil crumbs and pushes the air out. Dry soil gives the most bubbles. This air is what roots breathe.

check.q: When you poured water on dry soil, bubbles came up. What does that show?
check.why: Soil has tiny gaps full of air. Water filled the gaps and pushed the air out. Roots need this air to breathe.

flow.do: 1. Put 3 spoons of soil into glass 2. 2. Fill it almost to the top with water. 3. Stir hard for half a minute. 4. Leave it somewhere it won't be knocked.
flow.say: Now we'll mix soil and water and leave it overnight. What do you think we'll see tomorrow? Why?
flow.kid: Put soil in the second glass. Add water. Stir hard. Guess what you will see tomorrow.

flow.do: Look at glass 2 from the side. Name the layers together.
flow.say: What do you see now? What sank to the bottom? What floated on top?
flow.kid: Look at the glass from the side. What sank? What floated?

ask.q: What is soil made of?
good: Little stones, sand and mud.
Bits of old leaves and roots.

flow.parent: Heavy bits sink first: small stones, then sand, then fine mud on top. Bits of dead leaves and roots float. Potting mix from a nursery often has lots of brown coco peat floating. Fine mud can keep the water cloudy for a day.

activities.title: My Plant's Five Needs: a picture map
activities.context: In this activity you draw one plant from your home in the middle of a page. Around the plant, you draw the five things they need, and where in your home each one comes from.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper and colour pencils
a plant at home, or your rai sprouts

schedule.what: Draw the plant and their five needs, and where each one comes from.

activities.record: The picture map is the record. Keep it with your sprout drawings.

setup.art: A child drawing a pot plant in the middle of a big paper sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your plant in the middle.

setup.art: The finished drawing: a plant in the middle with five arrows to a window with a sun, a tap, swirls of air, a warm sun-patch and a pot of soil.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the five needs around them, and where each comes from.

flow.do: Draw the plant in the middle of the sheet with your child.
flow.say: Let's draw our plant in the middle. Now, what does this plant need to live?
flow.kid: Draw your plant in the middle of the page. What does your plant need?

ask.q: What does the plant need?
good: Light
Water
Air
Warmth
Soil

flow.do: Around the plant, draw the five needs: light, water, air, warmth and soil. Draw where each one comes from in your home.
flow.say: Where does our plant get light from? And water? Who gives the water? Where does the air come from?
flow.kid: Draw the five needs around your plant. Where does each one come from?
flow.parent: Good answers name real places: the window for light, the tap and you for water, the open window for air, the sunny days for warmth, and the pot for soil. Some children add a sixth need: someone who cares for the plant. That is a good thought.
flow.think: Which need does your plant get without anyone's help?

games.title: Five Needs: grow your plant to a flower
games.context: This is a card game about the five needs of a plant. Each player collects light, water, air, warmth and soil for their own plant. Trouble cards can take a need away.

items.f: Light: a sunny window
items.b: Your plant can make food in their leaves.

items.f: Light: a bright balcony
items.b: Leaves use light to make food, even on a balcony.

items.f: Light: morning sun through the grille
items.b: A little morning sun is enough for leaves to make food.

items.f: Water: one spoon a day
items.b: Your plant's leaves stay firm.

items.f: Water: the monsoon rain
items.b: Rain gives water, and the roots take it in.

items.f: Water: a drink from a steel tumbler
items.b: Roots take in water from the soil.

items.f: Air: an open window
items.b: Leaves take in a gas from the air to make food. Roots breathe too.

items.f: Air: a pot with a hole at the bottom
items.b: Extra water drains away, so the roots get air.

items.f: Air: a fresh breeze
items.b: Leaves take in a gas from the air to make food.

items.f: Warmth: a warm day in Chennai
items.b: Your plant grows well in enough warmth.

items.f: Warmth: a sunny afternoon
items.b: Warmth helps a plant grow.

items.f: Warmth: the end of winter
items.b: When it gets warmer, seeds sprout and plants grow faster.

items.f: Soil: a pot of good soil
items.b: Roots hold on and take in minerals.

items.f: Soil: manure from the nursery
items.b: Manure adds minerals to the soil.

items.f: Soil: soil from under a tree
items.b: Roots hold on to the soil and take in minerals.

items.f: Light: a sunny verandah
items.b: Leaves use light to make food.

items.f: Water: a watering can on Sunday
items.b: Water keeps the leaves and stem firm.

items.f: Air: loose soil with gaps
items.b: The roots breathe the air in the gaps in the soil.

items.f: Warmth: a warm morning in Kochi
items.b: Seeds sprout fast and plants grow well in enough warmth.

items.f: Soil: compost made from vegetable peels
items.b: Compost adds minerals to the soil.

items.f: Trouble: someone shuts your plant in a cupboard
items.b: Give back a Light card. In the dark, a plant cannot make food.

items.f: Trouble: the family goes to Madurai for a week, and nobody waters
items.b: Give back a Water card. A plant wilts without water.

items.f: Trouble: the pot is filled to the top with water every day
items.b: Give back an Air card. Soggy soil has no air, and roots can rot.

items.f: Trouble: frost in a cold Shimla winter
items.b: Give back a Warmth card. Frost can kill tender leaves.

items.f: Trouble: the plant is growing in a cup of plain sand
items.b: Give back a Soil card. Sand has few minerals.

rules: Each player draws a plant sheet: a pot with five empty boxes around it, labelled Light, Water, Air, Warmth and Soil, and a flower at the top. Shuffle the 25 cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top card. Read the front aloud, then turn it over and read the back aloud.
If it is a need card and your box for that need is empty, put the card in the box. If you already have that need, put the card at the bottom of the pile.

If it is a Trouble card and you have the need card it names, give that card back. Put the Trouble card, and the card you gave back, at the bottom of the pile. If you do not have that need card, just put the Trouble card at the bottom.
When all five of your boxes are full, colour in your flower and say the five needs aloud. Then you stop taking turns.
The game ends when every plant has flowered. Everyone wins together. There are 4 cards of each need, so every player can always find the one they are missing.

setup.art: Three children around a table, each with a paper sheet showing a pot and five empty boxes, and a pile of cards in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Each player gets a plant sheet. Cards go face down in the middle.

setup.art: A plant sheet with all five boxes filled with cards and a coloured flower at the top.
setup.caption: 2. Fill all five boxes to make your plant flower.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 25 cards. 2. Each player draws a plant sheet with a pot and five boxes. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
flow.say: Your plant needs five things to flower. Can you guess what they are? Let's find out as we play.
flow.kid: Look at your plant sheet. There are five boxes. Each box is a need.

flow.do: Take turns turning over cards. Read the front and then the back aloud. After each Trouble card, ask why.
flow.say: That is a Trouble card. Why does that hurt the plant? Which card do you give back?
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Read it. Is it a need or a trouble?

ask.q: Why does filling the pot to the top with water every day hurt the plant?
good: The roots can't get air.
The roots can rot.

flow.do: When a player's plant flowers, they say the five needs aloud.
flow.say: Your plant has flowered. Tell us the five needs.
flow.kid: Say the five needs: light, water, air, warmth, soil.

check.q: Which one is NOT one of a plant's five needs?
check.why: Plants make their own sugar in their leaves. The five needs are light, water, air, warmth and soil.

games.title: Follow the Light: a sprout game with a torch
games.players: 2 or more: a grown-up is the Sun, the children are the sprouts
games.context: This is a moving game. The children are sprouts, rooted to one spot. A grown-up is the Sun and shines a torch from different places. The sprouts must turn towards the light, slowly, without moving their feet.

items.f: The Sun shines from the window
items.b: Turn slowly to face the window.

items.f: The Sun shines from the door
items.b: Turn slowly to face the door.

items.f: The Sun shines from straight above
items.b: Stand up tall and stretch upwards.

items.f: Night: the Sun is gone
items.b: Stay still and rest. Sprouts keep growing slowly at night.

items.f: A cloud covers the Sun
items.b: Stay where you are. Wait for the light to come back.

items.f: Someone turns your pot round, so the light is behind you
items.b: Keep your feet still. Slowly turn your top half round to face the light.

items.f: The Sun shines from your left
items.b: Lean slowly to your left.

items.f: The Sun shines from your right
items.b: Lean slowly to your right.

items.f: Someone puts a box over you
items.b: Crouch down low in the dark. Then stretch up slowly, tall and thin. When the Sun lifts the box and shines the torch, open your arms like leaves and face the light.

rules: Each sprout picks a spot and keeps their feet still all game. A sprout cannot walk. The Sun needs a torch or a phone light.
The Sun turns over a card, reads the front aloud, and shines the torch from that place. If the card says night, switch the torch off.
The sprouts turn or lean as slowly as they can. A sprout who moves a foot, or turns fast, stands up straight and starts that card again.
After each card, the Sun reads the back, and the sprouts say why they moved that way.
When all the cards have been read, swap so a child becomes the Sun.

setup.art: Three children standing still with arms up like leaves, as a grown-up holds a torch near a door.
setup.caption: 1. Sprouts stand still. The Sun holds the torch.

setup.art: The same children slowly leaning their top halves towards the torch, feet still.
setup.caption: 2. Sprouts turn slowly towards the light.

flow.do: Cut out the 9 Sun cards. Each sprout chooses a spot. Remind them their feet stay still.
flow.say: You are rai sprouts. Your roots hold you in one spot. You cannot walk. You can only grow towards the light, slowly.
flow.kid: You are a sprout. Keep your feet still. You can only lean, slowly.

flow.do: Read a card, shine the torch from that place, and watch the sprouts turn. After each card, ask why.
flow.say: Why did you lean that way? How would a real sprout do that without muscles?
flow.kid: Lean towards the light, slowly. Why did you lean that way?

ask.q: How does a real sprout lean, without muscles?
good: By growing more on one side.
The shady side grows longer.

flow.do: Make the card about the turned pot the last one you read.
flow.say: A real rai sprout turns back to the window in about a day. You turned in a few seconds. What is different about a real sprout?
flow.kid: A real sprout turns back to the window in about a day. How is a real sprout different from you?

ask.q: What is different about a real sprout?
good: They turn by growing, not by moving their feet.
They are much slower.

projects.title: Straight or Bent? Two trays of rai to eat
projects.context: In this project you grow rai sprouts in two trays by the window. You turn one tray round every second day, and never turn the other. After a week you compare them, then snip the sprouts and eat them.

materials.item: rai (mustard) seeds
2 small trays, or old plastic boxes with a few holes poked in the bottom, each standing on a plate
kitchen tissue folded into 4 layers and wetted, or clean cocopeat
materials.qty: enough for 2 cm in each tray

materials.item: a spoon and water
clean kitchen scissors

schedule.what: Fill both trays. Scatter the seeds thickly. Water. Put both trays by the window, and label them TURN and STAY.
Water both. Turn the TURN tray round.
Water both. Turn the TURN tray. Look at both trays from the side.
Water both. Turn the TURN tray. Draw both trays.
Compare the trays. Snip the sprouts, wash them and add them to curd rice, a sandwich or a salad.

projects.record: Draw both trays from the side on day 6 and day 8.
projects.safety: A grown-up snips the sprouts with the scissors. Wash the sprouts well before eating.

setup.art: Two small plastic trays of soil on a windowsill, labelled TURN and STAY, with mustard seeds scattered thickly on top.
setup.caption: 1. Sow two trays. Label them TURN and STAY.

setup.art: On day 8: the TURN tray with sprouts standing straight up, and the STAY tray with sprouts all leaning to the window.
setup.caption: 2. Turn one tray every second day. Compare on day 8.

flow.do: 1. Fill both trays with wet folded tissue, or 2 cm of cocopeat. 2. Scatter 1 tablespoon of seeds on each. 3. Water both. 4. Label them TURN and STAY. 5. Put them side by side by the window.
flow.say: We will turn the TURN tray round every second day, and never move the STAY tray. How do you think they will look after a week? Why?
flow.kid: Fill two trays. Scatter seeds. Water them. Guess how each tray will look in a week. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The STAY tray will lean to the window.
The TURN tray will keep bending back and forth.
The TURN tray will grow straight.

flow.do: Every second day, water both trays and turn the TURN tray round. Look at both trays from the side.
flow.say: Look at the two trays from the side. How are they different?
flow.kid: Water both trays. Turn the TURN tray. Look from the side.
flow.parent: The STAY tray leans more and more towards the window. The TURN tray bends one way, then the other, and grows mostly upright. This is why gardeners turn indoor pots now and then.

flow.do: 1. Compare the trays. 2. Snip the sprouts just above the soil. 3. Wash them. 4. Add them to curd rice, a sandwich or a salad.
flow.say: Which tray grew straight? Why? Now let's taste our rai. Is the taste mild or sharp?
flow.kid: Which tray grew straight? Why? Now taste the sprouts.

ask.q: Why did the TURN tray grow straight?
good: They kept bending back to the light from both sides, so it evened out.

flow.parent: Mustard sprouts taste a little sharp and peppery, like the seeds. A grown-up does the snipping.

challenges.title: The Maze Box: can a shoot find the way out?
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. You build a dark box with one hole and a wall inside it. Then you see if a sprouting potato can grow round the wall to reach the light. It may take one to three weeks, and it does not always work. If the shoot has not reached the hole after three weeks, that is a result too.
challenges.problem: Make a box that is dark inside except for one hole. Put a sprouting potato at the far end, behind a wall. Can the shoot find a way round the wall to the hole?
constraints: Use a shoebox or any cardboard box with a lid.
Only one hole may let light in.
Put at least one cardboard wall between the potato and the hole.
materials: cardboard and sticky tape for the inside wall
a potato that is already sprouting little shoots, from the kitchen basket
a small cup of damp soil to sit the potato in
scissors, for a grown-up to cut the hole
general: Cut a hole about the size of a coin in one end of the box. Tape a cardboard wall halfway across the middle, with a gap at one side. Put the potato at the far end and close the lid.
Stand the box with the hole facing a bright window.
creative: Add a second wall with a gap on the other side, so the shoot must zig-zag.
Use a long box, like a shoe box for boots, to see how far the shoot will grow in the dark.
Make a box with two holes, one big and one small, and see which hole the shoot chooses.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own maze. Draw it first. Check it every 3 days, and close the lid quickly. How many days did your shoot take to reach the light?

setup.art: An open shoebox with a coin-sized hole in one end, a cardboard wall taped halfway across inside, and a sprouting potato in a cup at the far end.
setup.caption: 1. Build the box: one hole, one wall, the potato at the far end.

setup.art: The same box opened after two weeks: a long pale shoot from the potato curving round the wall and poking out of the hole.
setup.caption: 2. After 1 to 3 weeks, the shoot finds the hole.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a coin-sized hole in one end of the box. 2. Tape a cardboard wall across the middle, with a gap on one side. 3. Put the potato in a cup of damp soil at the far end. 4. Close the lid and tape any gaps.
flow.say: The shoot will be in the dark. Only one hole lets light in, and there is a wall in the way. Do you think the shoot can find the hole? Why?
flow.kid: Build the box with a grown-up. One hole, one wall. Put the potato at the far end. Guess: will the shoot find the hole?
flow.parent: A potato that already shows small shoots works best. The potato does not need much water, because they carry their own food and water.

flow.do: Every 3 days, open the lid for a moment and look. Close it again quickly.
flow.say: Where is the shoot now? Which way is the shoot growing?
flow.kid: Open the lid quickly. Where is the shoot? Close the lid.
flow.wait: Check every 3 days for 1 to 3 weeks.
flow.parent: The shoot will be long, thin and pale, because it is dark inside. That is normal. The shoot grows towards the faint light coming round the wall.

flow.do: When the shoot reaches the hole, open the box and look at the whole shoot together.
flow.say: Look at the path the shoot took. How did the shoot know which way to grow?
flow.kid: Look at the shoot's path. How did the shoot find the way?

ask.q: How did the shoot find the way?
good: The shoot grew towards the light.
A little light came round the wall, and the shoot followed it.

challenges.safety: Do not eat a sprouting potato or its shoots. They can make you ill. A grown-up cuts the hole. Wash hands after touching the potato.

items.p: Sort these into two groups: what a plant needs, and what a plant does not need.
cats: A plant does not need this
items: A plant does not need this
A plant does not need this
A plant does not need this
items.why: The five needs are light, water, air, warmth and soil. Plants make their own food, so they do not need biscuits or juice.
items.art: Eight small pictures: a sun, a water drop, swirls of air, a warm thermometer, a pot of soil, biscuits, a television and a glass of juice.

items.p: Draw a line from each need to why a plant needs each one.
pairs: To make food in the leaves
To keep the leaves and stem firm
So the leaves can make food and the roots can breathe
To hold the roots and give minerals
items.why: Each need does a job. Light, water and air are used to make food. Water keeps the plant firm. Soil holds the roots and gives minerals.
items.art: A sun, a water drop, swirls of air and a pot of soil on one side, four small pictures of the jobs on the other.

items.p: A plant eats the soil, the way we eat food.
items.why: False. Plants make their food in their leaves, using light, air and water. The soil gives them water and minerals.

items.p: Label the parts of this rai sprout: root, stem, leaves. Then draw an arrow to show which way the sprout will bend.
items.a: Root at the bottom, stem in the middle, two leaves at the top. The arrow points towards the window.
items.why: The stem is the part that bends towards the light. A strong answer puts the arrow towards the window, not towards the room.
items.art: A large mustard sprout with blank labels, and a window drawn on the left side.

items.p: Write one reason why a flower pot has a hole in the bottom.
items.a: So extra water can drain out, and the roots can get air.
items.why: A pot full of water has no air in the soil, and roots need air to breathe. The hole lets extra water out.

items.p: Which one does NOT help a plant grow?
opts: A shut cupboard with no light
items.why: In the dark, a plant cannot make food. The others all give a plant what they need.

items.p: A plant growing towards light is called ______. Say the word aloud, and a grown-up can write it for you.
items.why: 'Photo' means light, and 'tropism' means turning. Phototropism is turning towards light by growing.

items.p: Two friends in Hyderabad look at a money plant leaning towards the window.

views.says: The fan blew the plant over, so the plant leans.
The plant grew that way, to get light.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you saw in the turning cup test. Then say a test Zoya could do to check her idea.
items.a: Revathi. In the turning cup test, the sprouts bent back to the window when we turned the cup. A fan would not make them do that. Zoya could switch off the fan and turn the pot, and see what the plant does.
items.why: A strong answer uses the turning cup result as evidence, and is fair to Zoya by giving her a real test to try.

items.p: Which plant needs the least water?
opts: Rice in a flooded field in Thanjavur
items.why: Different plants need different amounts of water. A cactus can go weeks without rain, but rice grows in fields full of water.

items.p: Pick two of the five needs. Write what happens to a plant if each one goes missing.
items.a: No light: the plant cannot make food. No water: the leaves go soft and droop.
items.why: A strong answer names two needs and says what goes wrong for each one. Other pairs are fine, for example no air, so the roots cannot breathe, or no warmth, so the plant grows very slowly.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last, for the turning cup test.
items: The tops bend back to the window
The sprouts lean to the window
a: The sprouts lean to the window
The tops bend back to the window
items.why: First the seeds germinate. As they grow, they lean to the light. Then we turn the cup. By the next day, the tops bend back.

items.p: Kalpana, a girl in Pune, puts a pot of sprouts inside a box with a hole on the left side. Draw how the sprouts will look in two days.
items.a: The sprouts bend towards the hole on the left.
items.why: The only light comes through the hole, so the sprouts grow towards it. A strong drawing shows them bending left, towards the hole.
items.art: An empty box with a small hole on the left side and a pot of seeds inside.

items.p: In the turning cup test, cup A had 12 rai sprouts. The next day, 10 of them had bent back to the window. How many had not bent yet?
items.a: 2 sprouts had not bent yet. 12 take away 10 is 2.
items.why: Not every sprout turns at the same speed. The 2 may bend by evening.

items.p: Your rai seeds sprouted on wet tissue with no soil. Where did the sprouts get their first food from?
items.a: From the food store inside the seed.
items.why: A seed carries a small store of food. The sprout uses that store until their leaves can make food in the light.

items.p: Malini, a girl in Coimbatore, has a tulsi plant that her grandmother waters every day. Malini's cousin Vinod says more water is always better.

views.says: More water is always better. Plants like water.
Damp is good, but a soaking pot is bad for the roots.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in the soil glass. Then say one thing the other person got right.
items.a: The grandmother. The bubbles showed that soil has air in it, and roots need that air. Too much water fills the gaps. But Vinod is right that plants need water, and they wilt without it.
items.why: A strong answer uses the bubbles as evidence that soil holds air, and admits Vinod's fair point.

items.p: Match each plant to the warmth they grow best in.
pairs: Hot all year, by the sea in Kerala
items.why: Each plant grows best in a different warmth. Coconuts like heat, mustard is sown in the cool winter, and apples need cold winters.
items.art: A coconut palm, a yellow mustard field and an apple tree, with a beach, a winter field and snowy hills.

items.p: Which gas do leaves take in from the air to make food?
items.why: Carbon dioxide is a gas in the air. Leaves take it in through tiny holes, and use it with water and light to make food.

items.p: Some farms grow lettuce with the roots in water and no soil. What must the farm add to the water?
items.why: Plants need minerals to keep growing. In soil they come from the soil. With no soil, the farm adds them to the water.

items.p: Frost can kill the leaves of many plants.
items.why: True. Frost is a thin layer of ice that forms on very cold nights. It damages the leaves of many plants.

items.p: The roots of mangrove trees in the Sundarbans stick up out of the mud. Why might this help the tree?
items.a: Mud has very little air. The roots that stick up can take in air from above the mud.
items.why: Roots need air. A strong answer links the sticking-up roots to the need for air, as in the bubbles from the soil glass.

items.p: In the Straight or Bent project, one tray was turned every second day and one was never turned. Which tray grew straight up, and why?
items.a: The tray that was turned. The sprouts bent one way, then the other, so the bends evened out and they grew upright.
items.why: A strong answer says the light kept changing sides, so no side of the stem grew faster for long.

items.p: Darshana, a girl in Guwahati, wants a pot plant on her table to grow straight and not lean. What should she do? Why?
items.a: Turn the pot a little every few days, so the light falls on each side in turn.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that plants grow towards the light, and that turning the pot evens it out.

items.p: Two scientists watch a rai sprout bend back towards the window.

views.says: The sprout felt where the light was and chose to grow towards it.
Light set off a chemical called auxin, and the stem bent. The sprout does the same thing every time, so the bend is a response, not a choice.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one fair thing about the other view.
items.a: Either side can be argued. Dr. Lalitha: the sprout sensed the light and acted on what they sensed, which is what minds do. Dr. Rahul: we can see the chemical steps, and the sprout always does the same thing.
items.why: This is a real disagreement. A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and says something fair about the other side, for example that Dr. Rahul's chemical steps are true, or that Dr. Lalitha is right that the sprout sensed the light.

items.p: A cup of rai is turned round, and a day later turned round again. Each time, the tops bend to the light. Draw one stem from the side. How many new bends does it have?
items.a: Two new bends, so the stem looks wiggly, like the letter S.
items.why: Each turn starts a new bend near the growing tip, and the older bends stay in the stem. So the stem keeps a record of where the light came from.

items.p: The Darwins put tiny black caps on the tips of some grass shoots. Those shoots did not bend to the light. What does that show?
opts: The tip is the part that senses the light
items.why: When light could not reach the tip, the shoot did not bend. So the tip senses where the light is, and a message travels down to the part that bends.

items.p: Three of these show a plant growing towards light. Which one does not?
opts: Rai sprouts bending to a window
A potato shoot growing to a hole in a box
A money plant reaching for a window
A root growing down into soil
items.why: Roots grow down, into the soil, away from the light. The others are all shoots growing towards light.

items.p: This is a pot cut in half. Label where the air is, where the water is, and where the minerals are taken in.
items.a: Air in the gaps between soil crumbs. Water in the damp soil and around the roots. Minerals are taken in by the roots, with the water.
items.why: Soil is not solid. It has gaps holding air and water, and the roots take in water and minerals from them.
items.art: A cut-away pot with soil crumbs, small gaps between them, roots, and blank labels.

items.p: Seeds sprouted on tissue as well as in soil. But after ten days, the soil plants were bigger. Explain both results.
items.a: At first both used the food store in their seeds, so both sprouted. When the store ran out, only the soil plants had minerals to keep growing.
items.why: A strong answer explains both days: the seed's food store first, and the soil's minerals later.

items.p: Sunflowers in full bloom turn to follow the Sun all day.
items.why: False. Young sunflower plants turn with the Sun. Once the flowers open, most stop turning and face east.

items.p: Shalini, aged 8, puts a tulsi in a sunny window and forgets to water the plant for a week. The leaves go soft and droop. She gives the plant water. What will most likely happen next?
opts: The leaves stand up again after a few hours
Nothing, the plant stays soft for ever
items.why: Water keeps the leaves firm. A plant that is only a little dry can stand up again after a drink.

quiz.p: A plant has water, air, warmth and soil, but is kept in a dark cupboard. Which need is missing?
quiz.why: The five needs are light, water, air, warmth and soil. In the dark a plant cannot make food. Plants make their own sugar, so they do not need sugar or milk.

quiz.p: Rai sprouts are growing by a window. Which way do they lean?
quiz.why: Young shoots grow towards light. The window is where the light comes from.

quiz.p: How does a sprout bend towards light?
opts: The sprout walks on their roots
The shady side of the stem grows faster
quiz.why: The side away from the light grows faster, so the stem bends towards the light. Light does not pull.

quiz.p: Rai seeds on wet tissue, with no soil, will most likely do what?
quiz.why: Seeds carry a little food store. With water, air and warmth they sprout, even with no soil.

quiz.p: Why do plants growing for many weeks need soil, or minerals in water?
opts: The seed's food store runs out, and the plant needs minerals
quiz.why: Plants make their food in their leaves, but they need minerals from the soil to stay healthy. They do not eat the soil.

quiz.p: Bubbles came up when we poured water on dry soil. What were they?
opts: Air from the gaps in the soil
quiz.why: Soil has gaps full of air. Water pushes the air out. Roots breathe this air.

quiz.p: Ranjini, aged 7, keeps her pot full to the top with water every day. What will most likely happen to the roots?
opts: They can rot, because they cannot get air
quiz.why: Roots need air as well as water. In soaking soil, water fills the air gaps.

quiz.p: Rai seeds are sown in a very cold room and in a warm room. Where will they most likely sprout first?
opts: Both at exactly the same time
quiz.why: Seeds germinate faster when it is warm enough for them. In the cold, they are slow.

quiz.p: Nisha, a girl in Class 2, wants to know if rai seeds need soil. She sows 10 seeds in soil by a window, and 10 seeds on tissue in a dark cupboard. What is wrong with her test?
opts: She changed two things: soil and light
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing only. If the seeds differ, she cannot tell if soil or light made the difference.

quiz.p: A potato is kept in a dark kitchen basket with a small gap of light at one side. Which way will the pale shoots grow?
quiz.why: Shoots grow towards light, even a small amount. The shoots are pale and long because it is dark.

applications: Gardeners turn pots on a windowsill every few days, so the plants grow straight.
Farmers sow each crop in the season with the right warmth: rice in the warm monsoon, and mustard and wheat in the cool winter in the north.
Pots have a hole at the bottom so extra water drains out and roots get air.
Some farms grow lettuce and herbs with their roots in water with minerals added, without soil. This is called hydroponics.
E. K. Janaki Ammal, a botanist from Kerala, worked at the sugarcane institute in Coimbatore from 1934, breeding sugarcane to suit Indian conditions.

open_questions.q: What is it like for a sprout to feel where the light is?
open_questions.why_open: Plants have light sensors, and they act on what they sense. Nobody knows what that feeling is like for a plant.

open_questions.q: How does a sprout know which side of their stem is shady?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that auxin moves to the shady side. How the sprout compares the two sides so exactly is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why do roots of some plants grow away from light?
open_questions.why_open: Roots of some plants, such as the mustard family, bend away from light in a lab. Scientists are still working out what this does for a plant in the soil.

jokes.j: Why did the money plant go to the doctor?

maths.problem: Uma, a girl in Kochi, sowed 10 rai seeds in a cup. By day 3, 7 had sprouted. How many had not sprouted yet?
maths.explain: 10 take away 7 is 3. Seeds do not all wake up at the same time, so some may sprout tomorrow.
maths.context: This is about the soil or no soil test.
maths.why_maths: Counting how many sprouted, out of how many we sowed, tells us if the seeds are good.

maths.problem: In the soil cup, 9 of the 10 seeds sprouted. On the tissue, 8 of the 10 seeds sprouted. Did soil make a big difference to sprouting? Why do you think so?
maths.answer: No, not a big difference. 9 and 8 are very close.
maths.explain: 9 is only 1 more than 8. One seed can fail by chance, so a difference of 1 does not show that soil matters for sprouting. A big difference, like 9 and 0, would.
maths.context: This is about the soil or no soil test.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers tells us if the difference is big enough to mean something.

maths.problem: Cup A's sprouts bent back to the window in 1 night. Nisha, a girl in Class 2, turned the cup round every night for a week. How many times did the sprouts turn back?
maths.answer: 7 times, one for each night of the week.
maths.explain: A week has 7 nights. If the sprouts turn back each night, that is 7 turns. The stem may end up wiggly, with a bend for each turn.
maths.context: This is about the turning cup test.
maths.why_maths: Counting the days helps us predict how many bends the stem will have.

maths.problem: On day 4, rai sprouts were 2 cm tall. On day 8 they were 6 cm tall. How many centimetres did they grow in those 4 days?
maths.explain: 6 cm take away 2 cm is 4 cm. That is about 1 cm each day.
maths.context: This is about the Straight or Bent project.
maths.why_maths: Measuring twice and taking away shows how fast the sprouts are growing.

roots.context: We have seen rai sprouts turn back towards the window after we turned their cup. Now we ask what that tells us about plants, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: When we turned cup A round, the rai sprouts bent back to the window by the next day. A plant cannot walk to the light, so they move by growing. Every bend stays in the stem. So a plant's shape shows where their light has come from.
deep_truth.habit: We split living things into those who move, like humans and other animals, and those who stay still, like plants. But plants move all the time, by growing, too slowly for us to see.
deep_truth.evidence: In the turning cup test, cup A's sprouts curved back towards the window overnight while cup B stayed as it was. In the Straight or Bent project, the tray turned every second day grew mostly upright, and the tray never turned leaned to the window.

three.who_am_i: Your body grows too, and your shape also shows how you have lived: the hand you write with, the way you stand.
three.what_is_life: Being alive means sensing what is around you and acting on it. The rai sprouts felt where the light was and grew towards it.
three.what_is_this_world: The world gives every plant light, water, air, warmth and soil. Each plant grows into a shape that fits the place they found.

roots.thread: A rai seed holds a tiny plant. Around that plant is the whole world: sunlight from far away, water from the tap and the rain, air from the window, warmth from the day, and soil from the ground. The sprout senses all of this and grows to meet the world. So each sprout's shape is made by the seed and the world together.

teachings.source: Acharanga Sutra, Book 1, Lecture 1, Lesson 5 (a Jain scripture)
teachings.teaching: As a human is born, so is a plant born. As a human grows, so does a plant grow. As a human needs food, so does a plant need food.
teachings.link: Our sprouts needed light, water, air, warmth and soil, as we need food, water, air and warmth. Jain teachers saw plants as living beings with needs, like us.

teachings.teaching: Plants are born soft and supple. When they die, they are dry and brittle.
teachings.link: Only a young, soft, growing shoot can bend towards the light. The bend in our rai sprouts happened near the tip, where the stem was youngest and still growing.

science.text: Plants have light sensors called phototropins, mostly sensitive to blue light. These tell a shoot which side the light comes from.
Plants feel where the light is and act on it. What that feeling is like for a plant, nobody knows yet.

other_view.view: Many plant scientists say a sprout bends because light moves a chemical, auxin, to the shady side, and that makes those cells grow longer. It happens the same way every time, so they call it a response, with no choosing.

practice.title: Grow towards the light
practice.say: Stand in the middle of the room, facing away from the window. Keep your feet still, like roots. Close your eyes. Can you feel which side is brighter or warmer? Now lean your top half towards the window, as slowly as you can. Take five slow breaths while you turn. Open your eyes. Did you face the light?
practice.kid: Stand with your back to the window. Keep your feet still. Close your eyes. Turn slowly to where it feels bright. Take five slow breaths. Open your eyes.

founder: ideas/by_topic/plants.md: Photosynthesis and vision row ('grow a potted plant in varying light and record growth'; 'light is life's bridge'). Its sunbeam dance was not used, because Level 3 of this unit has a seedling dance; the torch game g2 uses the idea of sprouts answering the light instead.

Leads on from Level 1 (methi in light and dark, plates) and leads to Level 3 (fair tests of light, water and warmth with moong). This level adds phototropism, air in soil, soil and warmth, with rai seeds.
science: Phototropism: shoots bend towards one-sided light because auxin is moved to the shaded side, where cells elongate faster (the Cholodny-Went model, widely accepted, details still studied). Any plant physiology textbook, for example Taiz and Zeiger, Plant Physiology.
Charles Darwin, assisted by Francis Darwin, The Power of Movement in Plants (London, 1880): canary grass (Phalaris canariensis) seedlings with their tips covered did not bend towards light.

Frits Went (1926 to 1928): diffusion of a growth substance from oat coleoptile tips into agar blocks, which caused curvature when placed on one side of a decapitated coleoptile. The substance was later named auxin.
Phototropins are blue-light receptors that start phototropism (Winslow Briggs and colleagues, 1990s).

Atamian, Creux, Brown, Garner, Blackman and Harmer, 'Circadian regulation of sunflower heliotropism, floral orientation, and pollinator visits', Science 353 (2016): young sunflowers track the Sun, mature flower heads face east, warm faster and get more pollinator visits.
Seeds germinate using their stored food; seedlings need mineral nutrients to keep growing (hydroponics shows soil itself is not needed).
Roots need oxygen; waterlogged soil leads to root rot. Pots have drainage holes for this reason.
Mustard (Brassica juncea) is a rabi (winter) crop in Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh.
E. K. Janaki Ammal worked at the Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Coimbatore, from 1934, breeding sugarcane varieties suited to Indian conditions.
Acharanga Sutra 1.1.5 (Jacobi's translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. 22): plants compared with humans in being born, growing and needing food.
Tao Te Ching 76: the living are soft and supple, the dead are hard and stiff; plants are tender when alive and dry when dead.
Potato shoots growing through a cardboard maze towards light is a standard school demonstration; it takes one to three weeks.
